hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when life feels too crowded, what do you do first?
options: good news: you already speak a little yiddish. listen.
then let this old story keep you company. listen.
then this rabbi’s advice will surprise you. listen.

steps.line: In a little village, a poor man lived in one tiny room with his wife, his mother and a houseful of children. It was loud. Very loud.
steps.label: a Yiddish folk tale

steps.line: So he went to the rabbi to kvetch, which is Yiddish for complain, at length. “Rabbi, it’s so crowded. What do I do?”
steps.label: a Yiddish folk tale

steps.q: The rabbi strokes his beard and thinks. What odd advice do you think he gives?
o: Bring your chickens into the house
Move the whole family into the barn
Invite your in-laws to come and stay
steps.why: Yes, really: the chickens. It’s an old Yiddish folktale, retold in a well-loved picture book, “It Could Always Be Worse.”

steps.line: “Do you have chickens?” asked the rabbi. “Bring them inside.” So the man did. Now it was louder, and full of feathers.
steps.label: a Yiddish folk tale

steps.line: He schlepped back, dragging his feet, to kvetch again. “Bring in the goat,” said the rabbi. Then, “Bring in the cow.” Oy vey.
steps.label: a Yiddish folk tale

steps.q: The rabbi keeps making it worse. What do you think he’s up to?
o: He’s testing whether the man will obey
He doesn’t really understand the problem
He wants the man to see his home differently
steps.why: He can’t make the house any bigger. He can change how it feels to come home.

steps.line: At last the rabbi said, “Now take them all out.” Out went the chickens, the goat and the cow.
steps.label: a Yiddish folk tale

steps.line: That night the family ate supper in the same little room. It felt so quiet, so roomy. “Rabbi,” said the man, “it’s wonderful.”
steps.label: a Yiddish folk tale

steps.q: Your week went badly, and a friend shrugs, “It could always be worse.” In this story’s spirit, what are they saying?
o: Look again at what you already have
Stop complaining; others have it harder
Brace yourself; things will get worse
steps.why: In the story it isn’t a scolding. It comes with a smile: not “your trouble doesn’t matter,” but “look again.”

steps.q: Match each Yiddish word to the moment it fits.
pairs: “The bus was late again, and don’t get me started…”
the cake slides off the plate
steps.why: Yiddish was the everyday language of Ashkenazi Jews in central and eastern Europe, built mostly on medieval German, with Hebrew and Slavic words mixed in. English kept a few.

say: here’s what i love. the rabbi never lectured. he listened, every single time, and found a way to make the man laugh at himself.
that’s a mensch: yiddish for a real human being, decent and kind. long before yiddish, the sage hillel taught: where no one is acting like a person should, try to be that person.

steps.q: The rabbi made life worse on purpose. Would the trick work if he’d just said, “Be grateful for your room”?
o: Yes: good advice is good advice
Probably not; he had to feel it
Yes, if the man trusted the rabbi
steps.why: Told to be grateful, the man would have nodded and gone home grumbling. A week with a cow in the kitchen, he felt it.

today.say: be a mensch in one small way today. an old jewish teaching says the wise don’t interrupt. when someone kvetches to you, listen all the way through, the way the rabbi did, before you offer any advice.
options: that’s a mensch. the rabbi would be proud.
ha. then thank whoever listens to you. that counts too.
